tldr: Instead of certifying the running controller, the authors propose a new framework that guarantees 'recoverability'—the ability to return to a trusted recovery mode—using contraction theory, preserving safety without restricting aggressive behaviors even at operating limits where models are least reliable.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of the proposed 'recoverability' approach. The robot normally runs aggressive maneuvers or learned policies (deployed mode) without any filtering, and switches to a formally certified recovery mode at the optimal timing just before safety is lost.
overview:
Robots deliver their best performance when operating right at the limits of their envelope, such as the edge of tire traction or skimming past obstacles. However, traditional safety certification (such as control barrier functions) relies on 'forward invariance'—requiring the active behavior to remain inside a safe set indefinitely. Because dynamic models are least reliable near these boundary regions, conventional approaches face a tough dilemma: certification either breaks down or forces overly conservative intervention that severely degrades performance.

To resolve this tension, the authors flipped the conventional perspective 180 degrees. Rather than demanding that the running controller stay invariant inside a safe set, they only certify that the robot can safely re-engage a trusted backup behavior when needed. They call this 'recoverability.' Using contraction theory, they mathematically prove that switching to the recovery mode from anywhere inside an offline-certified recovery tube guarantees exponential convergence to a safe reference trajectory, even under disturbances and model error.

Furthermore, they derive the 'contraction insertion gradient (CIG)' to determine when to switch, embedding it into a 1D optimization program where feasibility alone guarantees safety while optimality merely tunes performance. Through simulated quadrotor flight and real-world rain testing aboard a full-scale IndyNXT autonomous racecar, the framework demonstrates superior performance over existing safety filters while providing rigorous safety.
contributions: Established the concept of 'recoverability,' demanding model fidelity only for the recovery mode rather than the deployed controller, and proving robust exponential convergence under disturbances.
Derived the contraction insertion gradient (CIG) and a switching-time program to decide online when to re-engage the recovery mode without sacrificing safety.

Developed a sequential convex synthesis method that monotonically grows certified recovery tubes toward the theoretical safe limit (HJ viability kernel) while maintaining closed-form distance functions for lightweight online evaluation.

Demonstrated real-time recovery on a full-scale IndyNXT autonomous racecar at the limits of handling on a wet track in the rain, successfully pulling the car back from an aggressive raceline to a safe trajectory.

sections.heading: Breaking the Performance-Safety Dilemma: The Counterintuitive Idea of Recoverability
sections.summary: Robots perform best near their operating limits, but traditional safety certificates break down in this high-uncertainty regime. This paper introduces an architecture that certifies 'recoverability' rather than invariance, leaving aggressive controllers completely unrestricted.
sections.details:
Whether it is high-speed drone acrobatics or drifting a racecar, robots unlock their highest performance right at the edge of hardware capabilities. Yet, attempting to push these limits runs headfirst into a fundamental wall imposed by conventional safety frameworks.

Existing safety certification tools, such as control barrier functions (CBF) and Hamilton–Jacobi (HJ) reachability analysis, are all built upon forward invariance: the deployed behavior itself must remain within a safe set indefinitely. Making this guarantee hold requires high-fidelity dynamic models throughout the safe operating envelope. However, boundary regimes—like tire friction limits or contact transitions—are notoriously difficult to model and lack rich data. In short, traditional guarantees are least reliable exactly where safety certification is most needed. Moreover, standard safety filters intervene as soon as the robot approaches the boundary, blunting the performance it was meant to deliver.

To overcome this, the authors introduce a fresh perspective: certifying safety does not require certifying the running controller itself. This is 'recoverability.' The deployed mode running day-to-day does not need to be linear, invariant, or even have a high-fidelity model. It can be a deep reinforcement learning policy or an intuitively tuned heuristic. Instead, the framework maintains a single offline-certified 'recovery mode' and monitors online only whether the system can safely transition back to it. This decouples aggressive performance from formal safety certification.

sections.heading: How Does It Differ from Existing Safety Filters and Backup Controllers?
sections.summary: HJ reachability analysis and CBFs impose heavy modeling burdens, while prior backup controller methods suffer from degraded performance during intervention and lack convergence guarantees. The proposed contraction-theoretic approach allows completely free execution right up to the intervention point.
sections.details:
Forward invariance has long been the gold standard for formal safety certification. HJ reachability analysis computes the exact maximal safe set, but suffers from an exponential computational explosion with state dimension. CBFs, while solvable online as lightweight quadratic programs (QPs), make designing valid barrier functions notoriously difficult. Predictive safety filters also rely heavily on model accuracy over long future horizons. Because all of these methods certify the actively running controller, aggressive maneuvers inevitably inflate the modeling burden.

To ease this requirement, backup controller frameworks (such as Simplex architectures and Backup-CBF) fix a safe fallback behavior. However, traditional Backup-CBF operates as a binary reachability test by forward-integrating the fallback trajectory into a target set, lacking explicit convergence rates or geometric safety margins. Furthermore, near boundaries, QP-based blending between normal and backup controls yields compromised, sluggish trajectories that follow neither the intended maneuver nor a clean fallback, imposing a persistent performance penalty.

Figure F2 highlights this contrast clearly. Running unconstrained (left) maximizes performance but eventually exits the safe set. Backup-CBF (middle) stays safe but pays a continuous intervention cost along the constraint boundary. In contrast, the proposed method (right) lets the aggressive behavior run at 100% fidelity right up to the edge of the certified recovery tube, and then contracts the system exponentially to the safe reference trajectory with a single optimal switch. High-fidelity modeling is required only around the recovery mode, leaving the deployed mode completely unconstrained.

captions.F2: Comparison of three control strategies. No intervention (left) maximizes performance but breaches safety. Backup-CBF (middle) preserves safety but continuously incurs intervention cost while constraints are active. The proposed approach (right) leaves the nominal behavior completely unhindered until the certified switching time $\tau^\star$, after which it exponentially recovers to a safe reference trajectory.

sections.heading: Capturing Safety Through Geometry: Contraction Metrics and Recovery Tubes
sections.summary: By modeling robot dynamics as vector fields and leveraging Riemannian contraction theory, the authors construct a 'recovery tube' around a trusted recovery trajectory, providing the geometric foundation for safe recovery from any state within the tube.
sections.details:
### III-A Closed-Loop Modes and Reference Consistency
The robot dynamics are represented by two closed-loop vector fields: the deployed mode $F_{\mathrm{new}}$ and the recovery mode $F_{\mathrm{rec}}$. Formulating behaviors as vector fields allows the framework to treat the controller as a black box, whether it is MPC or a neural network. The recovery target is a reference trajectory $\mathbf{x}_r(t)$, which the authors require to satisfy 'reference consistency': the reference itself must be an exact solution of the recovery mode ($\dot{\mathbf{x}}_r(t) = F_{\mathrm{rec}}(\mathbf{x}_r(t), t)$). The deployed mode does not need to track this reference at all and remains free to pursue its own objectives.

### III-B Recovery Contraction Metric and Recovery Tubes
To measure trajectory divergence, a Riemannian metric $\mathbf{M}(\mathbf{x},t)$ is defined over the state space. Contraction theory analyzes the property where infinitesimal deviation vectors shrink exponentially over time. When the Jacobian $\mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{rec}}$ of the recovery mode and the metric differential satisfy a specific matrix inequality, the metric is called a 'recovery contraction metric (with rate $\gamma > 0$).'

This metric induces the 'recovery tube $\mathcal{T}_r$', defined as the set of states where the Riemannian recovery energy $\mathcal{V}_{\mathbf{M}} = \frac{1}{2} d_{\mathbf{M}}^2$ from the reference trajectory remains below $E_{\max} = \frac{1}{2}r^2$. As long as the robot remains inside this tube, offline geometric analysis formally guarantees that switching to the recovery mode will reliably draw the system back to the reference trajectory.

sections.heading: When to Switch: Contraction Insertion Gradients and Safety by Feasibility
sections.summary: The authors prove exponential convergence upon switching from anywhere inside the tube and derive the Contraction Insertion Gradient (CIG). This formulation decouples safety from optimization: finding any feasible switching time fully guarantees safety.
sections.details:
### IV-A Proof of Contractive Recoverability
The authors first prove that switching to $F_{\mathrm{rec}}$ from any state inside the recovery tube $\mathcal{T}_r$ ensures that the Riemannian distance $L(t)$ to the reference trajectory decays exponentially at rate $\gamma$ (Theorem 1). More importantly, they establish robustness against real-world disturbances and modeling errors. Even under an unmodeled disturbance $d$, as long as its bound satisfies $\bar{d} \leq \gamma r$, the robot cannot escape the tube and tracking errors remain strictly bounded (Theorem 2). This provides a crisp geometric margin: as long as the contractive restoring force at the boundary ($\gamma r$) exceeds the disturbance bound ($\bar{d}$), invariance is guaranteed.

### IV-B Contraction Insertion Gradient (CIG)
How does the system decide exactly when to switch during nominal operation? The key is the Contraction Insertion Gradient (CIG). The energy gradient $\rho_{\mathbf{M}}$ can be computed instantly in closed form from the terminal velocity of the Riemannian geodesic. Taking the inner product of this gradient with the vector field difference $\Delta F = F_{\mathrm{rec}} - F_{\mathrm{new}}$ gives the exact first-order sensitivity of the recovery energy to an infinitesimal recovery insertion. When $\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{M}} < 0$, inserting recovery immediately decreases recovery energy, whereas a positive gradient indicates that switching is counterproductive.

### IV-C and IV-D Switching-Time Optimization and Decoupled Safety
Over a predicted planning horizon, the system identifies the first tube exit time $\tau_{\mathrm{exit}}$ and solves a 1D optimization problem to select the optimal switching time $\tau^\star$ prior to exit. A key result here is Theorem 3: 'feasibility alone guarantees safety.' As long as the selected switching time lies in the feasible set inside the tube, formal safety is preserved even if the optimizer has not converged to the optimum. Optimality merely shapes switching smoothness and performance, cleanly isolating safety guarantees from optimization challenges.

### IV-E Quadrotor Obstacle Avoidance Under Uncertainty
The framework was validated in simulation on a quadrotor navigating through uncertain ellipsoidal obstacles. The deployed mode planned aggressive high-speed trajectories based on optimistic obstacle estimates, while the recovery mode maintained a conservative path outside the maximal obstacle envelope. While a standard CBF collided with the real obstacle and Backup-CBF took an overly cautious, slow detour (reaching the goal at 6.718 s), the proposed recoverability filter maintained the aggressive flight plan until the very last moment, executing a single clean switch before the boundary to reach the goal safely in 5.206 s.

captions.F3: Simulation results of a quadrotor navigating an obstacle of uncertain size. (a) CBF collides with the true obstacle, and Backup-CBF takes a wide, slow detour, while the proposed method maintains the fast plan until the last moment, avoiding collision with a single safe switch. (b) Goal error trajectories. (c) Tube energy $\mathcal{V}_q$ profile, showing a switch triggered before exceeding the boundary (1.0) followed by rapid contraction.

sections.heading: Growing the Safe Envelope: Automated Recovery Tube Synthesis via Sequential Convex Programming
sections.summary: While tubes can be given a priori, larger tubes allow bolder robot actions. By introducing transport metrics with closed-form distances and applying sequential convex programming, the authors monotonically expand certified tubes toward the theoretical limits of the HJ viability kernel.
sections.details:
### V-A Transport Certificates with Closed-Form Distances
Computing Riemannian distances on general manifolds typically requires solving two-point geodesic boundary value problems online, which is computationally prohibitive. To bypass this, the authors introduce 'transport certificates' via a diffeomorphism $\mathbf{z} = \Phi(\mathbf{x})$ into a latent coordinate space. By choosing $\Phi$ such that the recovery dynamics become linear and the metric takes an ellipsoidal form in latent space, the physical geodesic distance evaluates instantly as a closed-form quadratic function. Furthermore, constraining the mapping to be volume-preserving ($\det D\Phi \equiv 1$) ensures that the latent ellipsoid volume directly matches the physical tube volume.

### V-B Tube Expansion via Sequential Convex Programming (SCP)
To maximize the tube volume within the safe set while preserving closed-form tractability, the authors formulate a sequential convex programming pipeline (Algorithm 1). The mapping $\Phi$ is constructed as a composition of volume-preserving shear maps, adding one shear transformation per step. Because volume expansion and contraction conditions can be structured as convex programs over boundary sample points, updates are accepted only after certifying global tube safety. This ensures the certificate is never violated while monotonically enlarging the tube volume step by step.

### V-C Rigorous Comparison with the HJ Viability Kernel
Using a planar error system with an unstable nonlinear drift, the synthesized tube $\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{syn}}$ was benchmarked against the exact Hamilton–Jacobi (HJ) viability kernel. Starting from an initial seed $\mathcal{T}_0$, eight shear iterations expanded the tube area by 107.3%, reaching 82.9% of the theoretical maximum provided by the HJ viability kernel. Unlike Backup-CBF sets that require forward trajectory integration, this synthesized tube evaluates membership via a single algebraic inequality. This achieves an expansive safe envelope near theoretical limits while keeping online computation virtually cost-free.

captions.F4: Synthesis results on a planar error model. (a) Evolution of the tube $\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{syn}}$ growing significantly from the seed $\mathcal{T}_0$ via successive shear maps. (b) Analytical set comparison: the proposed tube (green) covers 82.9% of the theoretical maximal safe set given by the HJ viability kernel $\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{HJ}}$ (purple). (c) Forward-time contraction of the sets toward the reference origin.

sections.heading: Flat Out in the Rain: Real-World Testing on a Full-Scale Autonomous Racecar
sections.summary: The proposed method was deployed on a full-scale IndyNXT racecar on a wet circuit—a severe, hard-to-model regime. Evaluating the CIG algebraically from onboard planner predictions, the system flawlessly recovered the vehicle across eight corner entries at the limits of handling.
sections.details:
### VI-A Real-Time Onboard Implementation
Deploying the theory on a full-scale IndyNXT racecar required execution within a ~10 Hz control loop. The authors defined a 2D lateral error coordinate system $\boldsymbol{\zeta} = [e_\perp, \dot{e}_\perp]^T$ relative to a conservative raceline. Adopting a diagonal metric $M_\zeta = \operatorname{diag}(0.5, 1.5)$ over this space turned the recovery energy into a simple algebraic evaluation, entirely removing the need for heavy online integration.

Both onboard controllers—the deployed mode running an aggressive racing MPC and the recovery mode tracking a conservative MPC line—broadcast predicted 5-second trajectories across 200 nodes. The recoverability monitor inspects these candidate trajectories and computes algebraic CIG values (Eq. 48) at each node. By incorporating an effective energy threshold $\bar{E}$ that accounts for a finite transition time ($\lambda = 0.5$ s), Algorithm 2 schedules an optimal switching time $\tau^\star$ just before the predicted trajectory leaves the recovery tube.

### VI-B Wet Track Deployment at Putnam Park Road Course
Field tests were conducted at Putnam Park Road Course under wet, low-friction track conditions where tire dynamic models are notoriously inaccurate. The vehicle reached speeds up to 20 m/s (~72 km/h). Because the car was fed a dry-weather aggressive raceline, it was repeatedly pushed toward the boundaries of the recovery tube upon corner entry.

Across a 30-minute continuous run, the system detected eight critical corner entries and triggered automatic transitions to recovery mode approximately one second prior to potential departure. As shown in Figure F5, the system initiated switching at $\tau^\star = 0.75$ s before the predicted energy breach, bounding lateral error and error rate within 0.5 m and 0.5 m/s, followed by smooth exponential decay to zero. The median lateral error before switching was 0.38 m, which contracted to 0.04 m after recovery. Crucially, on straights and stable segments where recovery was unnecessary, the deployed controller ran completely unhindered at 100% intended performance.

captions.F5: Hardware experiments with the IndyNXT racecar at Putnam Park in the rain. (a) Track layout showing aggressive candidate rollouts (dashed red) drifting wide before being recovered (blue). (b) Predicted energy profile over the planning horizon, deciding a switch at $\tau^\star=0.75$ s well before predicted tube breach at $\tau^V=1.68$ s. (c) Convergence of lateral tracking error around switching. (d) Error distributions before and after recovery across eight intervention events.

sections.heading: Conclusions and Future Outlook: Reframing Safety as an Exit Strategy
sections.summary: Recoverability reframes safety from a restrictive constraint on normal operation into a reliable exit strategy. Future work will focus on certifying re-entry conditions back to deployed modes and enabling safe reinforcement learning directly on hardware.
sections.details:
This work represents a key milestone in dismantling the 'curse of invariance' that has long compromised performance under formal robotic safety certificates. By shifting the verification requirement away from the deployed controller and focusing solely on the ability to transition into a trusted recovery mode, robots can operate with unconstrained freedom in regimes where modeling is least reliable.

Several promising directions lie ahead. First, the current framework implements a one-way transition: once recovery is triggered, the system stays in recovery mode. Establishing formal re-entry conditions that allow the robot to safely hand control back to the aggressive deployed mode after sufficient contraction will enable fully autonomous cycles between high-performance exploration and safe recovery.

Second is diversifying recovery options. By maintaining a library of certified recovery tubes—such as emergency braking, hovering, or righting maneuvers—the system can dynamically select the most context-appropriate escape route. Furthermore, this paradigm offers an ideal foundation for safe reinforcement learning (Safe RL) on physical hardware. With a certified recovery tube acting as a safety net, neural policies can aggressively explore boundary limits on hardware without risk of catastrophic damage. Viewing safety as an exit strategy rather than an operational constraint points toward an exciting future for autonomous robotics.

takeaways: Switching safety guarantees from 'maintaining invariance of the running controller' to an 'exit strategy that ensures reachability to a trusted recovery behavior' enables safety certification even in hard-to-model operating limits.
Contraction theory provides mathematical proofs for exponential convergence upon switching from within the certified tube, along with an explicit disturbance rejection margin ($\gamma r$).
Feasibility alone guarantees formal safety in the switching-time optimization program, while optimality merely shapes performance and smoothness, preventing real-time computational failure.

Sequential convex programming using volume-preserving shear maps expands certified recovery tubes close to theoretical limits (HJ viability kernel) while preserving closed-form distance evaluations for lightweight online execution.
limitations: Formal re-entry conditions to transition safely back to the aggressive deployed mode after completing recovery have not yet been established.

The strength of the overall safety guarantee relies heavily on the offline contraction metric and model accuracy of the recovery mode, still requiring rigorous modeling of the recovery behavior itself.

The full-scale racecar deployment relied on a 2D lateral error projection and first-order approximations for fast computation, treating complex 3D chassis and attitude dynamics as unmodeled disturbances.
